claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a single-phase solid solution.
Maintenance of the single-phase solid solution from 473 to 1923 K is primarily governed by kinetically limited atomic diffusion.
Reducing nanoparticle size increases the surface-to-volume ratio.
Reducing nanoparticle size enhances diffusion barriers.
Specific surface-capping agents enhance diffusion barriers.
Enhanced diffusion barriers delay the onset of phase segregation.
Nanoparticle size affects intrinsic atomic mobility.
Surface passivation by capping agents creates extrinsic barriers to diffusion.
Smaller nanoparticle size reduces effective diffusion paths.
Reduced effective diffusion paths kinetically hinder atomic rearrangement.
Kinetic hindrance of atomic rearrangement maintains a uniform, high-entropy, single-phase structure at high temperature.
Smaller, tailored-capping nanoparticles will segregate at a higher onset temperature than standard-size nanoparticles with unmodified surfaces under identical conditions.
Smaller, tailored-capping nanoparticles will show delayed compositional inhomogeneity relative to baseline particles at temperatures up to 1923 K.
Sufficiently extreme temperature or reactive conditions can activate significant atomic diffusion despite size reduction and surface capping.
When the imposed kinetic barriers are overcome, phase segregation may occur.
The effects of size reduction and capping on diffusion barriers may depend on multimetal composition and processing variations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the size effect to enhanced diffusion barriers, whereas the mechanism invokes shorter effective diffusion paths as a source of kinetic hindrance. Path shortening is not explained as a barrier-enhancing process, leaving the proposed size-dependent causal direction internally incoherent.
